title: Motion Dynamics Learning for Few-Shot Embodied Adaptation
one_liner: A robot learns new tasks with few examples by extracting and reusing patterns of how movements evolve over time, rather than just copying individual actions.
lead: Vision-language-action models (systems that take pictures and text commands to control robot arms) need many task examples to learn something new. This paper says: those models waste information. The real treasure is how actions flow together in a sequence—the motion patterns. By learning those patterns once and reusing them, robots can adapt to new tasks with just 20 examples instead of hundreds.

paras: A trained vision-language-action model can see a picture and understand a command. But when you ask it to do a new task (like "pick up a red cup instead of a blue one"), it struggles. So you show it examples: "here's what picking up a red cup looks like." You show it 50, 100, 200 examples until it learns.

The problem: each example is treated as a standalone action. "Pick up, move right, release" — the model treats each motion independently, like three separate pictures. But in reality, those three motions form a single flow, a sequence where each step flows naturally from the last. A model that copies individual actions misses that the second motion wouldn't make sense without the first.
A beginner would just feed more examples. But that scales poorly: every new task demands hundreds of fresh examples. The model has to start almost from scratch each time.

callout.html: Learn how movements evolve together as sequences, store those patterns in a library, and build new task motions by mixing patterns from the library.

panels.title: 1. What the model sees
panels.caption: Picture + text command: pick up the red cup. Three independent actions.

panels.title: 2. The old way: copy actions
panels.caption: Model learns each action separately. No sense of how they connect.

panels.title: 3. The paper's insight: patterns flow

steps.text: Take a full example trajectory (pick up, move, release). Reverse-engineer the invisible pattern that generated it.
The pattern becomes a compact list of numbers representing the motion's essence (not the raw coordinates).
Collect patterns from hundreds of diverse demonstrations. Group similar patterns. Each pattern in the library represents a reusable motion primitive.

steps.b: Step 4: Constrain new tasks to the library
steps.text: When learning a new task, the model can only generate actions by mixing patterns from the library. This forces it to reuse what it already knows.
With just 20 new examples, the model learns which library patterns to blend and how to blend them for the new task.

object.h2: What changes: from actions to motion codes
paras: Instead of learning individual actions, the system learns codes—compact numbers that capture the essence of how an arm should move. When the model needs to act, it picks codes from a library and activates them, rather than generating raw action coordinates from scratch.

hidden.h2: The motion pattern: a learned representation of trajectory evolution
hidden.name: motion dynamics code
paras: A motion dynamics code is a compact list of numbers (learned during training) that captures the essence of how an action sequence should flow: the typical rising and falling of joint speeds, the relationship between different arm movements, the rhythm. It is not the trajectory itself—those are raw coordinates. It is the hidden pattern that, when combined with a specific task context, generates sensible trajectories.

The paper estimates it via flow-matching inversion: given a real trajectory, a neural network learns to reverse-engineer the code that would have produced it. You show the finished motion and ask, 'what code generated this trajectory?'

heat.caption: Darker codes matter more for generating believable motion sequences. Lighter codes are rarely activated.

reads.html: A motion code is the hidden recipe for how an arm should move: the timing of speed changes, the coordination between joints, whether movements should be smooth or jerky. It's learned from examples and stored in a library.

Motion dynamics codes are hidden numerical representations distilled via flow-matching inversion. They span a learned space where similar trajectories cluster close together, and the arrangement captures the structure of valid motions.

mechanism.h2: Why reusing motion codes makes few-shot learning work
paras: A robot's arm movements are not random. When you pick up something, there are only a few sensible ways to do it: smooth and careful, or quick and confident. The arm rarely jerks between extremes. This structure is the motion prior—knowledge built into how movement works.

The paper's insight: instead of forcing the model to learn this structure from scratch for each new task, learn it once from hundreds of demonstrations, store those learned structures, and then reuse them. When a new task arrives with only 20 examples, the model doesn't have to invent motion patterns. It just learns which stored patterns to activate and how to blend them.

Because the library already contains realistic motion patterns, the model can learn a new task's motion behavior from fewer examples. The 20 examples only need to teach, 'for this new scenario, blend pattern A at 70%, pattern B at 30%, and blend them like this.' That is far easier than learning the motion patterns themselves from 20 examples.

stages.s: Invert each example to its motion code
Decompose each code into library patterns
Learn the blend weights for this task

math.words: The motion generation score is the distance between the inferred code and the library, weighted by task-specific blend factors. The learning goal minimizes this distance while keeping the blend factors simple.
symbols: the motion code extracted from a single example
the k-th motion pattern stored in the library
how much to use pattern k for this new task (learned from the 20 examples)
a penalty that encourages using fewer patterns (keeps the blend simple)
the squared distance (how far apart two codes are)
the sum of all blend weights (counts how many patterns are active)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose one example trajectory inverts to code z_inferred = [3.0, 2.0, 1.0]. The library holds three patterns: z_1 = [2.8, 2.1, 0.9], z_2 = [3.2, 1.8, 1.1], z_3 = [2.9, 1.9, 1.2].
The model tries blend weights w = [0.6, 0.4, 0.0]. It constructs library blend = 0.6 * [2.8, 2.1, 0.9] + 0.4 * [3.2, 1.8, 1.1] = [2.96, 2.04, 0.96].
Total loss: 0.0048 + 1.0 ≈ 1.00. Lower blend weights or match the library better to reduce loss.

math.note: The equation forces the inferred codes to lie on the library, measured as weighted combinations of stored patterns. A low penalty on the sum of blend weights means the new task is built from as few library patterns as possible.

charts.title: Old way: action imitation
charts.note: Without structure, the model needs many examples to learn realistic trajectories. Motion patterns are invisible to it.

charts.title: This paper: motion code reuse
charts.note: With a library of motion patterns, even 20 examples are enough. The model reuses learned structures.

items.html: If the library was trained on only a few robot arms or scenarios, it might not contain patterns for a very different new task. The model cannot blend patterns it has never seen.

items.b: New task is unlike the training examples.
items.html: If the new task requires a motion pattern the library has never seen (for example, movements under water where drag is high), and the library was trained only on air, the model cannot build it from library patterns. The 20 examples are not enough for it to learn something completely new.

If the 20 examples are clumsy or unnatural (the demonstration was sloppy), flow-matching inversion may extract a distorted code that does not align well with the library. The model then fits the wrong pattern.
The library is diverse (many robot types and scenarios), the new task is a reasonable variant, and the 20 examples are clean and representative. The model learns quickly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple embodied task: a simulated arm reaching to different colored cups. Pre-train a motion library on 500 diverse reaching and grasping examples (use at least 5 different cups, 5 positions, 2 arm speeds). Then present the system with a new variant it has never seen (for example, a smaller or larger cup). Give it 20 labeled examples of this new variant. Measure success rate: can the arm reach and grasp the new cup.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (number of successful grasps) / (number of test attempts)
demo.closing: The demo must show that with 20 examples, the system solves the new variant faster than a model without a motion library would solve it with 50 examples, because the library provides ready-made motion structure instead of forcing the model to discover it from scratch.
